title: Christianity: the Lord's Prayer
hook: the prayer Jesus taught his followers (Matthew 6:9–13)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Beatitudes. Your line was blessed are the peacemakers. Did one softer word go into one tense place? Day two hundred fifty-five.

Our Father, who art in heaven. Those six words travel a long way from any church: into school halls, hospital rooms, gravesides and old films. Catholics, Orthodox Christians and Protestants all pray what follows, each in their own language and their own version, with small differences in the wording. And it all began with a simple request. In Luke's Gospel, the disciples watch Jesus pray and ask him: teach us. Today: the prayer he gave them.
screen: `OUR FATHER, WHO ART IN HEAVEN.` → `CATHOLIC, ORTHODOX, PROTESTANT.` → `TEACH US.`

segments.voice: Matthew chapter six, in the King James Version: "Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread." Then forgiveness, as we forgive others; then protection from temptation and evil. It's short on purpose. Just before it, Jesus warns against heaping up words, as if length impressed God. Look at the shape. The first half faces God: the name, the kingdom, the will. The second half faces us: bread, forgiveness, protection. Big things, then small things, and the small things are allowed in the same breath. Now today's line. Daily bread. It sounds simple, but the Greek word translated daily, epiousios, appears almost nowhere else in all of Greek writing, and nobody is certain what it means. Daily? For tomorrow? Needed for existence? Early Christian writers already argued about it, and some read it as the bread of the Eucharist too. However it's translated, the request is small: enough for today. Not a year's supply. It echoes the manna in the wilderness, from the story of the going out from Egypt: bread that came each morning, enough for that day, and spoiled if hoarded. Christians pray it in different forms. Many Protestants end with for thine is the kingdom, the power and the glory. Luke's version doesn't have that line, and at Catholic Mass it comes a little later, after another short prayer.
screen: `TEACH US TO PRAY.` · `GOD'S NAME FIRST, THEN OUR BREAD.` · `EPIOUSIOS — NOBODY IS SURE.` · `ENOUGH FOR TODAY, LIKE MANNA.` · then, large: `DAILY BREAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read it slowly once. If you pray, you can pray it; if not, simply listen to the old words. Our Father which art in heaven. Pause. Hallowed be thy name. Pause. Thy kingdom come. Give us this day our daily bread. Then sit with that one line. What is enough, just for today? The bell holds the time.
Christianity, through the Lord's Prayer: the prayer Jesus taught, God's name first, then bread for today. Today's word.
Your line: daily bread. Today, at one meal, notice that it's enough, and let tomorrow's worries wait until tomorrow. Day two hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Christians all pray the Lord's Prayer, many daily, and congregations often say it together; Catholics call it the Our Father and pray it in the rosary.

trapdoor: what you thought: the prayer from funerals and films.
what it means: the prayer Jesus taught: God's name and kingdom first, then bread, forgiveness and protection.
what a scholar hears: epiousios is nearly unique in Greek; Luke 11 has a shorter form, and the doxology is a later addition to Matthew's text.

The hook uses the liturgical 'who art in heaven'; the teach quotes KJV 'which art'. Intentional.
